articles.title: Após mortes, rodovia recebe lombadas e será duplicada em Itapira | G1
articles.standfirst: Duplicação de 16 km da Rodovia Comendador Virgolino de Oliveira deverá começar no início de 2027. Uma das lombadas instaladas fica no trecho onde primo da noiva morreu.
articles.summary: Duplicação de 16 km da Rodovia Comendador Virgolino de Oliveira deverá começar no início de 2027. Uma das lombadas instaladas fica no trecho onde primo da noiva morreu.
articles.body:
Imagem de arquivo da Rodovia Comendador Virgolino de Oliveira, em Itapira — Foto: CNT

Após as mortes de recém-casados e do primo da noiva, em acidentes de trânsito ocorridos em maio de 2026, a concessionária Arteris Intervias instalou lombadas eletrônicas e confirmou a duplicação da Rodovia Comendador Virgolino de Oliveira (SP-352) , em Itapira (SP).

Paola Talhatelli , de 18 anos, e Mathias Ambrosini , de 20, morreram no dia 21 de maio . Já o primo de Paola, Ronaldo Aparecido Vidal , de 50 anos, faleceu em 28 de maio . As tragédias tiveram grande repercussão.

De acordo com a Intervias, as lombadas eletrônicas, que forçam os motoristas a desacelerar, foram instaladas nos kms 173, sentido Jacutinga (MG), e 174, sentido Itapira. Uma delas, inclusive, fica no exato trecho onde Ronaldo sofreu acidente e morreu .

Já a duplicação de 16 km da estrada está confirmada e deverá começar no início de 2027, segundo a concessionária. "Estamos em fase de elaboração do projeto executivo para apresentação para Artesp, já temos o projeto funcional", completou.

Em junho de 2026, o g1 noticiou que a Intervias pediu à Agência Reguladora de Serviços Públicos Delegados de Transporte do Estado de São Paulo (Artesp) permissão para instalar novos radares na rodovia. Essa solicitação, no entanto, ainda não teve resposta e está sob análise.

Ronaldo Aparecido Vidal (à esq.), de 50 anos, primo da noiva (à dir.), morreu em uma colisão na mesma estrada — Foto: Reprodução/Redes sociais

O pedido da Intervias para instalar radares vai ao encontro de uma cobrança da mãe de Paola, Taiara Talhatelli, em entrevista ao g1 . Segundo Taiara, por conta do nivelamento de alguns trechos da rodovia, motoristas excedem o limite de velocidade .

"Ali, naquela descidinha que foi o acidente [de Ronaldo], em frente à empresa Cargill, se ficar cinco minutos vocês vão ver que os caminhões não descem a menos de 120 ou 130 km/h. Eles aproveitam a descida e soltam o caminhão carregado. [...] É conhecida como a 'rodovia da morte' aqui em Itapira", disparou.

"Essa pista aqui, como eu já comentei, ela é boa, realmente é sinalizada, porém é uma pista que precisa muito de radar", completou.

O casal foi velado e enterrado junto em 23 de maio, no Cemitério Parque Municipal da Paz, em Itapira. Centenas de pessoas passaram pelo local para prestar homenagem.

Por sua vez, Ronaldo foi velado em 30 de maio, no Velório Municipal Barão de Ataliba. O enterro ocorreu no Cemitério da Saudade de Itapira.

As tragédias que atingiram a família geraram comoção nas redes sociais . Após o acidente de Ronaldo, Comentários postados no Instagram do g1 Campinas definiram a situação como "dor incalculável para a família".

"Que Deus possa consolar os corações dos familiares. Uma dor incalculável para os familiares e amigos"

"Meu Deus! Deus continue confortando os corações dos amigos e familiares"

"Que o Senhor cuide do coração dessa família!"

articles.summary: Pesquisa divulgada neste sábado (3) é a última antes do 1º turno, neste domingo, e foi encomendada pela Globo.
articles.body:
Montagem mostra Cleitinho Azevedo (Republicanos), Patrus Ananias (PT) e Alezandre Kalil (PDT) — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Pesquisa Quaest divulgada neste sábado (3), véspera do 1º turno, mostra como está a disputa pelo governo de Minas Gerais. Cleitinho Azevedo (Republicanos) lidera com 54% das intenções de votos válidos. Em seguida, aparecem Patrus Ananias (PT), com 23%, e Alexandre Kalil (PDT), com 10%.

Infográfico mostra cenário de votos válidos no 1º turno na disputa ao Governo de MG na pesquisa da Quaest 03/10/2026 — Foto: Arte/g1

É a forma como o TSE divulga o resultado oficial das eleições. São os votos dados nos candidatos. Esse cálculo deixa de fora os votos em branco e os votos nulos. Para vencer no 1º turno, um candidato precisa de 50% dos votos válidos mais um voto.

A Quaest leva em consideração as intenções de voto da pesquisa e o perfil de comparecimento para estimar os votos válidos. É o modelo likely voter , que considera eleitores com maior propensão a votar .

O levantamento foi encomendado pela Globo e ouviu 3.204 eleitores de 16 anos ou mais, entre os dias 2 e 3 de outubro. A margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos. O nível de confiança é de 95%. A pesquisa foi registrada na Justiça Eleitoral sob o número MG-06889/2026.

Veja agora o resultado com os votos totais, incluindo votos em branco, nulos e eleitores indecisos.

Cleitinho Azevedo (Republicanos): 45% (eram 37% em 29 de setembro)

Professor Túlio Lopes (PCB): 0% (era 1%)

Branco/nulo/não vai votar: 12% (eram 9%)

Infográfico mostra cenário de votos totais no 1º turno da disputa ao Governo de Minas na pesquisa Quaest de 03/10/2026 — Foto: Arte/g1

Veja agora a pesquisa espontânea, em que os eleitores respondem sem ter acesso a uma lista de candidatos.

Esses resultados ajudam a medir o grau de consolidação do voto. Quanto maior o número de indecisos na véspera, menos consolidado está o voto e maior a possibilidade de mudanças em relação ao resultado de domingo.

Professor Túlio Lopes (PCB): 0% (era 0%)

Entre os eleitores que declaram voto em um candidato, 81% dizem que a decisão é definitiva. Outros 18% afirmam que ainda podem mudar de ideia.

Escolha é definitiva: 81% (eram 69% em 29 de setembro)

Muito interessado: 38% (eram 31% em 29 de setembro)

articles.title: Avião médico com 6 pessoas a bordo desaparece na costa leste dos EUA | G1
articles.standfirst: Aeronave havia saído das Bermudas e tinha Boston como destino, segundo autoridades. Guarda Costeira ainda buscava por avião, um Gulfstream G100 que transportava dois membros de uma equipe médica, um paciente e um parente dele.
articles.summary: Um avião de evacuação médica com seis pessoas a bordo, vindo das Bermudas e com destino a Boston, desapareceu neste sábado (3) em frente à costa leste dos Estados Unidos.
articles.body:
Em imagem de arquivo, um avião da Gulfstream, empresa da aeronave que desapareceu perto dos EUA — Foto: Gulfstream News

Um avião de evacuação médica com seis pessoas a bordo, vindo das Bermudas e com destino a Boston, desapareceu neste sábado (3) em frente à costa leste dos Estados Unidos , informaram a Guarda Costeira e a empresa responsável pela aeronave.

A Guarda Costeira afirmou, em uma publicação na rede social X, que navios e aeronaves estavan procurando o avião, um Gulfstream G100, ao longo da costa de Nantucket, em Massachusetts.

A aeronave, operada pela Latitude Air Ambulance, sediada no Canadá, desapareceu por volta de 1h30 da madrugada (2h30, pelo horário de Brasília), disse à agência de notícias AFP o porta-voz da empresa, Clarence Togeretz.

"Ela transportava dois pilotos, dois membros da equipe médica, um paciente e um familiar", declarou Togeretz, acrescentando que não tinha mais informações sobre as operações de resgate.

A empresa conta com uma frota de dez aviões que prestam serviços de repatriação e evacuação médica, levando as pessoas de volta para casa a partir de qualquer lugar do mundo, segundo seu site.

articles.title: In 2017, Cape Town turned 42 abandoned grain-silo tubes into a major African art museum and added a 28-room hotel above the old concrete structure
articles.summary: Discover how Cape Town's iconic grain silo complex was transformed into the Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art Africa and The Silo Hotel, showcasing innovative adaptive reuse of industrial heritage while preserving its historical character.
articles.body: For decades, a giant grain-silo complex rose over Cape Town's harbour, a monument to the city's industrial heritage. By 2017 the silo's storage tubes had become the Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art Africa, and the elevator tower above them housed a hotel. The change focused on 42 closely packed concrete silo tubes. Designers didn't tear down the original structure; they carved into it, creating galleries and public spaces within its unusual shape.The museum opened in September 2017 with around 9,500 square metres of custom-designed space spread over nine floors, according to Heatherwick Studio. The Silo Hotel, which occupies six floors of the elevator tower, has 28 rooms and suites. The project was a high-profile example of adaptive reuse, taking an old industrial building and turning it into a new cultural and commercial hub while retaining much of its original concrete construction.Why the old grain silo matteredThe silo was originally built as a storage and grading complex for maize that passed through Cape Town's working harbour. Heatherwick Studio, which spearheaded the renovation, said it was decommissioned as containerised transportation changed the way supplies were handled. What made the edifice most remarkable was a block of 42 closely packed silos. The complex had stood disused since 1990, leaving a huge concrete structure with no industrial purpose. The designers chose to keep its industrial character rather than demolish it and start afresh.This presented an architectural problem. A grain silo is built around narrow, cylindrical storage tubes, not rooms with traditional walls, windows and floors. The approach was to carve new niches into the concrete and to remove selected parts so the tubes could assist in shaping the museum’s galleries and central atrium. The approach also maintained the history of the structure visible. Externally the building still looked like an industrial building, but internally it had been renovated into a museum for contemporary African art and its diaspora.Carving a museum from concreteThe existing silo structure was excavated to create the galleries and atrium, exposing the geometry of the 42 tubes. It was more than a superficial facelift. To make functional exhibition spaces, large parts of the internal concrete had to be ripped out and rebuilt, while leaving enough of the original structure to keep it standing.Adaptive reuse has gained importance as cities face ageing industrial buildings and is described as a way to keep existing structures in use while adding social, economic and environmental value. For historic grain elevators in particular, choosing a new use means balancing heritage value, investment interests and community needs [link]. Zeitz MOCAA was a particularly clear example of that challenge. A further study on the reuse of historic grain elevators concluded that determining the new use of such structures requires balancing heritage value, investment interests and community requirements. Zeitz MOCAA was a particularly obvious example of the challenge.A hotel stands above the galleriesThe role of the top half of the complex was significantly different. The Silo Hotel occupies six floors of the former grain elevator tower above the museum, according to Dezeen, and has 28 rooms and suites. Its exterior became one of the most visible parts of the makeover. The studio inserted pillowed glass windows into the tower's existing concrete frame, bulging outward in soft shapes that contrast with the hard concrete around them.The hotel opened first, in March 2017, several months before Zeitz MOCAA opened to the public in September. Together, the two uses turned a former industrial complex into a hotel, museum and public space. ... Instead, it incorporated the silo itself into the experience, with the original concrete tubes framing the galleries and the industrial shell still visible.What the silo becameThe Cape Town project shows what adaptive reuse may be when the most challenging aspect of a building becomes its distinctive feature. The same thin tubes that had originally contained grain formed the core of a museum interior, while the elevator tower above held a 28-room hotel. Research on industrial history increasingly sees such buildings as assets to reuse, rather than just sweep them away. In Cape Town the method saved a bit of the working heritage of the harbour while providing the structure for two very different new duties. The result was not a copy of the original silo but a new building within it: a museum with 80 gallery spaces and a rooftop sculpture garden, organised around an atrium that exposes the cut concrete tubes.You use AI every day. articles.title: Elon Musk's baby mother Ashley St Clair says it's 'karmic' that Shivon Zilis 'got played' after what she did to Grimes
articles.summary: Conservative influencer Ashley St Clair who mothered a child with Elon Musk before being cut off from his life reacted to Shivon Zilis' announcement of a
articles.body: Conservative influencer Ashley St Clair who mothered a child with Elon Musk before being cut off from his life reacted to Shivon Zilis' announcement of a sudden break up. Ashley expressed mixed emotions after going through Zilis' statement of being abandoned by Musk in a week and noted that it was kind of 'karmic', though she is a girl's girl and would be there for Shivon if she reached out to her, she said in her Instagram stories.Zilis and Ashley, however, were not the same to Elon, as he called Shivon his partner for a long time and they share four children, the oldest one being born in 2021.Reading between the lines of Shivon's social media post, Ashley said it was obvious that Elon Musk had cut her off like he generally does and so the announcement was Shivon's only way to reach Elon Musk. Ashley said it struck as pretty odd that Shivon wrote that she and their children were Elon Musk's respite, as this should not happen. "Children should not be emotional comfort for damaged men," Ashley said. "It should be the other way round, parents should be children's comfort."Ashley said she felt bad reading Shivon's post because Shivon seemed to be groveling and the post read like a "trauma bond" but she said she understood immediately that Shivon had no other way to communicate with Elon as further communications only happen through attorneys.Ashley said her understanding of the situation was that it did not happen in a week; there had been moves to separate and disentangle her from his life for a month. But Shivon claimed to be blindsided. Ashley said it was kind of karmic because Shivon pretended to be Grimes' friend but went behind her back to make secret children with Elon. Ashley said Grimes was blindsided by Shivon when her surrogate was giving birth to her and Elon Musk's child while in the same hospital, Shivon was also giving birth to her and Elon's child.Elon Musk- Grimes-Shivon Zilis- Ashley St ClairIt's a complex web of overlapping relationships.Elon Musk's first wife was Canadian author Justine Wilson. They married in 2000. The couple had six children, although their first son, Nevada Alexander, died of sudden infant death syndrome at 10 weeks old in 2002. They had twins Griffin and Vivian in 2004 and triplets Kai, Saxon and Damian in 2006. The marriage ended in 2008.Soon after their divorce, Musk began dating British actress Talulah Riley. They married in 2010 in Scotland. The relationship ended in divorce in 2012, but the two reconciled and remarried in 2013. Musk filed for divorce again in December 2014 but withdrew the filing. Riley subsequently filed for divorce in 2016.After Riley, Musk and actor Amber Heard became romantically involved after Heard's marriage to Johnny Depp ended. Their relationship was on-and-off between 2016 and 2018.Musk and Canadian musician Grimes publicly revealed their relationship in 2018. They had three children together. Their first child, X Æ A-Xii, was born in May 2020. Their second child, Exa Dark Sideræl, was born via surrogate in December 2021. A third child, Techno Mechanicus, was later reported to have been born in 2022.It overlapped with Musk's relationship with Shivon Zilis as Musk and Zilis welcomed twins, Strider and Azure in November 2021. In 2024 and 2025, they had their third and fourth -- Arcadia and Seldon Lycurgus.This again overlapped with Musk's relationship with Ashley as Ashley announced in February 2025 that she had a child with Musk.You use AI every day. articles.title: Four North Carolina homes damaged by Helene were repaired with owners’ money and volunteer help; two years later, FEMA buyouts mean the livable houses will be demolished and returned to green space
articles.summary: Two years after Hurricane Helene devastated western North Carolina, four homes that owners worked to repair after the storm are now set to be demolished.
articles.body: Two years after Hurricane Helene devastated western North Carolina, four homes that owners worked to repair after the storm are now set to be demolished. The homes, in Hendersonville’s Cottages at Cypress Run neighbourhood, were among properties damaged by the September 2024 storm and were rebuilt with homeowners’ own money and help from volunteers. According to the North Carolina Department of Public Safety (NCDPS), 535 of 892 homes in areas prone to repeated flooding have so far been approved for voluntary acquisition through the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program. Properties bought through the programme are removed, with the land returned to natural areas to reduce future flood risk.Homes repaired after Helene now face demolitionHurricane Helene brought catastrophic flooding to western North Carolina on September 27, 2024. NCDPS says the storm caused nearly $60 billion in damage across the state, damaged or destroyed more than 73,000 homes and resulted in 107 deaths. Two years later, the state says recovery remains ongoing.In Hendersonville, the consequences of that recovery process are now particularly visible at The Cottages at Cypress Run. Nearly half of the homes in the neighbourhood flooded during Helene. According to WLOS, four homes on Leyland Circle have since been repaired but are now scheduled to be demolished after their owners accepted voluntary FEMA buyouts.Charlene Olsen, one of the homeowners, told WLOS that about three feet of water filled her home during the storm. She said she and her dog returned to find the property covered in mud. Olsen later rebuilt the house using her own money and volunteer assistance, as did other neighbours. Despite the work that went into restoring the property, Olsen accepted a buyout. She told WLOS that she did not feel comfortable returning to the home after what happened during Helene. “I’m happy for the people that feel safe living there, but I don’t,” Olsen said.How the FEMA buyout programme worksThe buyouts are part of a broader hazard-mitigation effort designed to reduce the risk of future disasters. NCDPS says the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program provides funding for measures that can reduce future losses following a disaster, including the voluntary acquisition of properties in areas vulnerable to flooding.Under the programme, homeowners voluntarily apply to have their property acquired. Once FEMA approves an eligible project, the state or local government can complete the purchase. NCDPS says properties acquired through the programme are generally purchased at their approximate value on the day before the disaster.After the purchase is completed, the home is demolished and the property is cleared. According to NCDPS, acquired land must remain as public open green space, prohibiting new structures. The agency explains that maintaining the land as open space can provide additional floodplain and help keep floodwater away from neighbouring properties. For the Hendersonville homeowners, this means a repaired house can still be removed if the property is acquired through the voluntary buyout process.Why repaired houses are still being removedThe timing has raised questions among residents because the houses are now described as livable after the rebuilding work. WLOS reported that some neighbours questioned why homes that had already been repaired could not instead be used for people who lost their houses in the storm. Resident Shawna Cordier told WLOS that demolition might have made more sense earlier, when the neighbourhood was still recovering, rather than removing a house that is now “perfectly livable.”The HOA president, Mike Modzelewski, also told WLOS that residents were concerned about the disruption that could accompany demolition and wondered whether the neighbourhood could again face debris and other problems similar to those experienced after Helene. FEMA, meanwhile, has explained the purpose of the buyout in terms of long-term flood-risk reduction. In a statement to WLOS, the agency said that once a homeowner accepts a buyout, the home will be demolished and the property deed-restricted. FEMA said the land will be returned to green space, which maintains natural floodplain functions and reduces or eliminates future disaster losses to properties.A wider shift from rebuilding to mitigationThe Hendersonville properties are part of a much larger post-Helene mitigation effort. NCDPS says 535 of 892 homes in areas prone to repeated flooding had been approved for voluntary acquisition as of September 25, 2026. The state says those homes will be removed and the land returned to natural areas. North Carolina has also submitted about $2 billion in applications to FEMA through its hazard-mitigation efforts. More than $200 million had been allocated for projects across western North Carolina before the application period closed, with another $1.8 billion expected, according to NCDPS.The state’s approach reflects a distinction between rebuilding a home after a disaster and reducing the likelihood of repeated losses at the same location. A homeowner may repair a structure and make it livable again, while officials may still determine that acquiring the underlying property is appropriate because of its flood risk.For the four Hendersonville homeowners, that process has created an unusual outcome: houses that survived Helene, were repaired and could be lived in again are now headed for demolition. Once the buyouts are completed and the structures removed, the properties will be maintained as open green space rather than rebuilt as homes.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Queensland dairy farmer Libby Rough opened just four campsites after drought forced her family to sell 40 cows; by January 2022, the riverside pitches had brought in more than A$50,000
articles.summary: When a severe drought forced Queensland dairy farmer Libby Rough to sell 40 cows, her family faced a frightening financial crisis.
articles.body: When a severe drought forced Queensland dairy farmer Libby Rough to sell 40 cows, her family faced a frightening financial crisis. Without the regular income from milk sales, everyday costs such as groceries and school fees quickly became hard to pay. To keep the farm going, Rough opened just four unpowered campsites along the river that runs through her dairy property near Kenilworth, in the Sunshine Coast hinterland. By January 2022, those four grassy sites had brought in more than A$50,000 in extra income. What began as an emergency step became an important financial lifeline for the family. Rough's experience is part of a growing trend across rural Australia. With changing weather, higher farm costs, and unstable commodity prices, farmers are turning to agritourism and private camping on their land to help keep family farms financially secure.Emergency decision born from droughtThe idea started because the family had little choice during one of the region's driest periods. As the pasture dried and the cost of feed rose, they had to reduce their herd. This meant losing a large share of their regular income from milk production. Speaking to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC), Rough described how serious the situation had become on the farm. "During the drought, and because we hadn't had a milk cheque for three months, we joined up to Youcamp to help pay for groceries and school costs," Rough told the ABC. Youcamp was an Australian private land camping platform that later merged with global outdoor booking company Hipcamp. It allowed landowners to advertise private camping spots for travellers who wanted quiet places away from busy commercial caravan parks.Simple setups yielding major returnsThe Rough family kept the camping setup simple and low impact. Instead of spending heavily on permanent buildings, costly facilities, or concrete camping areas, they offered basic natural sites along the riverbank for campers who could look after themselves. The response was quick. By August 2020, demand for outdoor stays had risen sharply as people travelling within Australia looked for outdoor breaks close to home. By January 2022, the four basic riverside campsites had earned the family more than A$50,000. The money went directly toward maintaining farm equipment and infrastructure, buying cattle feed, and paying household bills during times when farming income was low. The extra money did more than help with immediate expenses. Hosting campers gave the family a financial cushion that helped them keep their remaining cattle and continue running the dairy farm through difficult seasonal periods.Industry sector gaining official momentumThe success of farms such as the Rough family's has attracted attention from industry groups and state agricultural agencies. As more regional landowners showed interest, the Queensland Farmers' Federation (QFF) published a discussion paper focused on the potential of farm tourism. The QFF said agritourism can give farmers another source of income. This can make regional businesses better able to cope with natural disasters, changes in trade, and climate shocks. Supporters say allowing farmers to host small numbers of campers needs little investment but can still bring wider benefits to local economies. People staying on farms often spend money at nearby bakeries, butcher shops, fuel stations, and country pubs. This helps spread their spending across small rural communities.Regulatory hurdles and council reformsEven with strong interest from farmers, planning rules have often made it difficult for landowners to start short-term accommodation businesses. Planning rules in many parts of Australia have required farmers to submit complex and expensive Development Applications (DAs) just to host a few caravans or tents on properties covering hundreds of acres. In many regional shires, council fees and other requirements made small camping businesses too expensive to operate. However, some local governments have started changing their approach. As reported by the ABC, councils such as Queensland's Gympie Regional Council took steps to reduce these barriers. In December 2021, the Gympie council voted to double the number of caravans or tents that could be hosted on private rural properties without requiring formal DA approval. Supporters of the changes say low-density, unpowered farm camping has a small environmental impact compared with traditional commercial developments. They also say this can work well when landowners properly manage basic sanitation and rubbish removal.Connect city visitors to local food originsFor many farmers, hosting campers has two benefits. It provides extra income while also giving farmers a chance to show city residents where their food comes from and explain the challenges of modern farming. People camping on working farms can see agricultural life up close. They may watch early morning milking, cattle being moved, and farmers caring for the land. As droughts continue to put pressure on the finances of traditional farms, small-scale agritourism is becoming more than a novelty. It is becoming a common way for farmers to earn extra money. For the Rough family, four simple riverside camping sites showed that a small piece of pasture can sometimes provide as much financial stability as a herd of dairy cows.You use AI every day. articles.title: Helicopters, influencers and nail art: The money trail of 2026 assembly elections
articles.summary: From paying social-media influencers to allocating money for 'nail art', the BJP's expenditure statements reveal the range of campaign activities funded
articles.body: From paying social-media influencers to allocating money for 'nail art', the BJP's expenditure statements reveal the range of campaign activities funded during its bid to win the West Bengal assembly election. A closer look at political parties' filings with the Election Commission of India (ECI) makes for interesting reading, revealing how spending priorities varied according to the political stakes in different states. However, the TVK example is only a humbling reminder that in democracy, greater outreach may lead to greater eyeballs, but it is no guarantee for success.The BJP declared Rs 529.39 crore expense for this year's assembly elections in West Bengal, Assam, Keralam, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry. Congress declared Rs 248.55 crore as spending, less than half that amount.A TOI analysis of the expenditure filings shows that Rs 178.78 crore of the Rs 280.84-crore difference, nearly two-thirds, came from advertisements and travel by star campaigners, the top leaders a party sends around a state to address rallies. Money given directly to candidates accounted for only Rs 16.27 crore of the gap. At least on paper, the BJP's extensive advertising campaigns and deployment of senior leaders, many of them massive crowd pullers, distinguished its expenditure pattern from that of Congress.The BJP won 207 seats in West Bengal in the results declared on May 4 and later won the Falta repoll to take its tally to 208. It formed its first government in the state, ending the Trinamool Congress's 15-year rule. TMC chief Mamata Banerjee lost her own seat, Bhabanipur, to the BJP's Suvendu Adhikari. The BJP-led NDA won Assam for a third consecutive term, while the NDA led by the All India NR Congress retained Puducherry.In Keralam, the Congress-led UDF returned to power after 10 years. Congress won 63 of the 140 seats, the CPI(M)-led LDF 35 and the BJP three. In Tamil Nadu, film star Vijay's TVK, contesting its first assembly election on the whistle symbol, won 108 of the 234 seats, ahead of the DMK with 59 and the AIADMK with 47. Subsequently, Vijay became chief minister.The campaign war chestsThe BJP, Congress and CPI(M) filed accounts covering all five elections, with the CPI(M) declaring only Rs 39.04 crore as expenditure. The DMK declared Rs 197.85 crore spending for Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, while the AIADMK reported Rs 112.40 crore expenses in a statement covering Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Keralam.TVK reported Rs 19.81 crore for Tamil Nadu, according to TOI report. TMC's full 2026 expenditure statement is not available on the ECI website.Political parties have no overall election expenditure ceiling, but individual candidates face spending limits. The accounts can also include expenditure authorised but not yet paid. The BJP's Bengal return, for instance, recorded Rs 89.32 crore in outstanding general-campaign expenditure at the end of the election period.Different states, different stakesMore than half the BJP's money, Rs 286.99 crore or 54.2 per cent, went to Bengal, followed by Rs 96.27 crore in Assam. Together, the two states accounted for Rs 383.26 crore, or 72.4 per cent of the party's total. The BJP also declared Rs 82.67 crore in Keralam, Rs 51.56 crore in Tamil Nadu and Rs 11.90 crore in Puducherry.The spending pattern broadly reflected the different political stakes.The figure broadly aligns with what was at stake too. BJP was desperate to get power in Bengal after catapulting to second position in 2021 and sensing anti-incumbency was heavily weighing down on Mamata Banerjee. In Assam, it was looking to consolidate a strong position. The party had much less at stake in Tamil Nadu where it is still an emerging force. In Keralam, a much smaller state than Tamil Nadu, more amount was pumped in sensing an opportunity to break the binary nature of the state politics.For Congress, the situation was totally different. Its biggest chance for coming to power was in Keralam and it’s no surprise that the party spent the most in Keralam, Rs 105.34 crore or 42.4 per cent of its total, followed by Assam at Rs 67.62 crore, or 27.2 per cent. It declared Rs 42.08 crore in Bengal, Rs 22.25 crore in Tamil Nadu and Rs 11.25 crore in Puducherry.Bengal accounts for most of the gap between the two parties, perhaps unsurprisingly, although both parties were contesting almost the same number of seats in the state. The BJP declared Rs 244.91 crore more than Congress there, about 87 per cent of the total difference. Keralam was the only state where Congress declared more, by Rs 22.67 crore.Ads, aircraft and the spending gapParty filings divide spending into different categories, and three of them help explain the BJP–Congress difference to an extent.The BJP declared Rs 187.54 crore on general-party media advertisements, which promote the party as a whole rather than individual candidates. Congress declared Rs 92.52 crore, a difference of Rs 95.02 crore.Star-campaigner travel covers trips by a party's senior leaders, and the BJP's schedules list aircraft and helicopter travel for several of them. The BJP declared Rs 106.25 crore under this head against Congress's Rs 22.49 crore, about 4.7 times as much and Rs 83.76 crore more.Direct grants, the money a party transfers to candidates, were much closer. The BJP declared Rs 111.79 crore and Congress Rs 95.52 crore, a difference of Rs 16.27 crore, with the BJP's grants about 17 per cent higher. Congress spent slightly more on grants than on general-party media advertisements.In Bengal, the BJP recorded grants of Rs 20 lakh each to its 294 candidates, totalling Rs 58.80 crore. In the same state, it declared Rs 88.48 crore on general-party media advertisements and Rs 52.18 crore on star-campaigner travel.Grants, however, are only part of the support candidates receive, since parties also pay centrally for publicity, rallies and other campaign activities.The difference extended beyond advertisements and star campaigners' travel. The BJP declared ₹52.34 crore on publicity materials, including posters, banners and flags, against Congress's ₹11.48 crore. Under other general-party expenses, the BJP recorded ₹48.83 crore against Congress's ₹6.78 crore, another ₹42.05-crore gap. Congress, however, declared more expenditure on general-party meetings and rallies, ₹7.99 crore against the BJP's ₹4.06 crore.From nail art to AI callsThe filings name the people and firms that were paid, though they do not always specify what services were delivered.In Bengal, the BJP's accounts include payments recorded against social-media influencers and content creators. TOI earlier reported that influencer Sayak Chakraborty acknowledged receiving Rs 2.5 lakh for two videos, The Bengal accounts also contain entries for nail art. Four entries of Rs 1 lakh each, marked "Nail Art", appear under public meetings and rallies. Another Rs 9.65 lakh is recorded against Visionary Edge for a "Nail Art Prog" under media advertisements.Sayak was not the only influencer or content creator named in the accounts. Others have also acknowledged receiving payments. Yet the separate virtual-campaign schedules recorded no expenditure.Across the five elections, the BJP's accounts list Rs 41.83 crore against Google India and Rs 15.65 crore against Facebook India Online Services, a total of Rs 57.48 crore, of which Rs 31.39 crore was attributed to Bengal. This amount is already included in the BJP's advertising expenditure. Advertising purchased through agencies for social media may also appear under other names.The filings also point to the use of artificial intelligence in election outreach. Congress's headquarters recorded Rs 3.72 crore against Neomarq Flare Solution LLP in Assam for a service described as "AI 2 Way Voice Calling".In Tamil Nadu, the DMK's Rs 197.85 crore included Rs 70.63 crore on general-party media advertisements and Rs 45.75 crore in grants to candidates. Five entries marked "Social media" added up to Rs 16.87 crore, naming Vipras Ads, Ravi Publicity Services, Glovy Trading and Populus Empowerment Network.Populus appeared four times in the accounts, for manpower and consultancy, campaign production, digital advertising (Rs 6.37 crore) and social media. Together, these entries totalled Rs 74.94 crore, about 37.9 per cent of the DMK's expenditure.The AIADMK recorded Rs 103.99 crore of its Rs 112.40 crore, or 92.5 per cent, in a single entry for Pramanya Strategy Consulting, described as "Social Media Promotion, TV, Website". Because the filing does not break down this amount, it cannot be compared directly with the DMK's specifically labelled social-media entries.The CPI(M)'s Keralam unit accounted for Rs 28.60 crore of the party's Rs 39.04 crore, and its Bengal unit Rs 8.23 crore. In Keralam, the party recorded Rs 19.53 crore on general-party media advertisements, of which Rs 18.77 crore, about 96 per cent, appeared in four entries naming Maitri Advertising for print, television and electronic media.These entries identify the companies named in the expenditure schedules, not necessarily the ultimate media outlets or platforms.When spending and seats divergedThe BJP won Bengal, the state where it declared its largest expenditure, while the Congress-led UDF won Keralam, where Congress spent the most.Tamil Nadu, however, presented a striking contrast.TVK reported expenditure of Rs 19.81 crore, including about Rs 6.3 crore on media advertisements, Rs 3.5 crore on Vijay's air travel and Rs 2.1 crore on public meetings and roadshows, according to TOI's September 26 report.The DMK declared Rs 197.85 crore across Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, while the AIADMK reported Rs 112.40 crore in a statement covering three jurisdictions. Although the reporting coverage differed, TVK's declared expenditure was substantially smaller than that of either established Dravidian party.Yet TVK won 108 assembly seats, compared with the DMK's 59 and the AIADMK's 47.Vijay entered politics with a considerable advantage in public recognition, having spent decades as one of Tamil cinema's biggest stars. His existing fan base and celebrity appeal may have given TVK organic visibility, yet the difference in spendings can’t be ignored.The filings offer a fascinating account of the financial machinery behind modern election campaigns, from helicopters and digital advertisements to influencers, consultants and AI-powered calls. They also expose the limits of pumping funds to win elections. Hence Tamil Nadu perhaps had the most important lesson for mainstream political parties.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1996, Indiana turned foundry waste sand into a 275-metre highway embankment; Purdue later found the material worked successfully as full-scale road fill
articles.summary: Explore how Indiana transformed industrial foundry waste sand into a successful highway embankment project in 1996, showcasing its effectiveness as a structural fill material and its environmental safety.
articles.body: In 1996, an unusual road-building experiment in Indiana gave an industrial waste product a second life. Instead of landfilling used foundry sand, the Indiana Department of Transportation (INDOT) and Purdue University used it to build part of a highway embankment near Butler. The project covered a 275-metre section of the Country Road 37 highway project and was designed to test whether waste sand from a metal foundry could perform as a structural fill material.According to Purdue e-Pubs, the experiment was more than a laboratory test. Engineers constructed the embankment at full scale and compared the foundry-sand section with sections made using conventional clay borrow and natural sand. The researchers monitored how the materials behaved during and after construction, examining settlement, strength, water movement and other engineering characteristics.From foundry floors to a road embankmentFoundry sand is reused in metal casting to make moulds and cores. However, once it is no longer useful in metal casting, large amounts of foundry sand may be treated as waste. The material used in the Indiana case study was supplied by Auburn Foundry Inc. in Auburn, Indiana. Instead of disposing of it, the material's engineering properties were investigated.According to Transportation Research Record, the 1996 demonstration used waste foundry sand from a ferrous foundry and included both WFS and control sections that were instrumented to monitor their geotechnical and environmental performance. The researchers found that the foundry sand had strength and deformation characteristics comparable to natural sand, supporting its use as structural fill. The demonstration was carried out on a full-scale section of highway embankment about 275 metres long, with engineers first constructing a test pad to determine how the material should be compacted and to assess its behaviour during construction.What happened when the waste was put to work?The scientists monitored movements within the embankment and changes in the material beneath it. Their observations involved both vertical and lateral deformations, pore water pressure, and penetration resistance. This provided a way of comparing the foundry sand layer with the other two layers of clay and natural sand. These findings were positive from a geotechnical point of view. The foundry sand displayed low internal deformations and high penetration resistance; its overall behaviour was similar to that of natural sand. It was concluded that, from the geotechnical point of view, foundry sand could be successfully used as an embankment material in highway construction projects.However, there were certain limitations to this approach. For one, the compaction of the foundry sand resulted in its low hydraulic conductivity compared to that of the natural sand, which means it could not be assumed to be a freely draining material. There was also a difficulty associated with the construction process due to the presence of foreign materials in the waste sand. Hence, foundry sand cannot be considered an appropriate substitute for all types of road building materials.Testing whether waste could become a resourceEnvironmental performance was yet another critical factor in the demonstration process. The testing included laboratory and field tests such as bioassays and analysis of metals and other elements, as the groundwater levels were monitored within the embankment area. The results showed that there was migration of some ions from the foundry sand, although concentrations were below the relevant regulatory thresholds. The researchers thus determined that no adverse environmental effects arose from using the material.This was another practical example of why the material deserved further study. Therefore, recycling the material would lessen the need for disposal and provide construction material. Research by the Recycled Materials Resource Center estimated that the Indiana project saved about $145,000 in material costs. The Indiana test did not imply that all foundry waste could be used on roads. Different foundries produce sands with different properties, so testing and quality control are still necessary. The case showed that an industrial waste material could be processed, tested and used in a real highway project to evaluate its performance. articles.body: NEW DELHI: A local court on Saturday granted bail to six Congress workers arrested for allegedly defacing the outer wall of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's ancestral home in Agra during a protest against alleged manipulation of voter lists.The accused - Mukesh Dhangar, Anil Yadav, Rajesh Kumar, Manoj Gaur, Rajesh Gautam and Pankaj Chaudhary - were granted bail after furnishing surety bonds of Rs 20,000 each, advocate Santosh Dixit, who represented them, said.The six were arrested on September 29 and had been sent to jail following a case registered against them under several provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, including those relating to attempt to murder, rioting, wrongful restraint and assault or criminal force against a public servant.Dixit said the police had dropped Section 109(2) of the BNS, relating to attempt to murder, after failing to substantiate the charge in its submissions before the court.In an earlier hearing, the court had directed the police to conduct a detailed investigation into the invocation of Section 109(1), asking them to specify the facts, injuries, medical evidence, eyewitness testimony or other evidence supporting the charge.The court had also directed the investigating officer to complete the probe by October 3 and drop the section if the investigation did not establish the alleged offence.On September 28 protest in which some Congress workers allegedly wrote slogans with black paint on the gate and outer wall of Kumar's residence in the Vijay Nagar area of Agra.Police registered the case at Hariparvat police station on a complaint by a sub-inspector against eight named persons and 15-20 unidentified Congress workers.The other charges in the case include Section 121 of the BNS, relating to voluntarily causing grievous hurt to deter a public servant from performing his duty, Section 126 on wrongful restraint and Section 132 on assault or criminal force against a public servant. Provisions relating to rioting, house-trespass, criminal intimidation and intentional insult were also invoked.Congress Agra city president Amit Singh welcomed the bail order and said the party would continue its agitation against Kumar."The serious section imposed by the police has been removed by the court. articles.title: ‘Will sign those checks’: Trump repeats $5,000 promise to US adults if Republicans win 2026 midterms
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has again promised to give every adult US citizen $5,000 if Republicans win control of both the House of Representatives and
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has again promised to give every adult US citizen $5,000 if Republicans win control of both the House of Representatives and Senate in the November midterm elections.In a post on X (formerly Twitter) on Saturday, Trump repeated the pledge, writing: “If Republicans win the House of Representatives and the Senate in the 2026 Midterm Elections, I’m going to give all Adult Citizens in the United States of America, $5,000.” He added: “I look forward to signing those checks!”Trump had first announced the proposed payment last month at the Republican Party’s midterm convention in Dallas, calling it a “Trump dividend”.He said at the time that Americans would receive the money if Republicans retained control of Congress.Trump has suggested that tariff revenues and what he describes as strong economic performance would help fund the payments. However, no detailed plan has been provided on how the checks would be financed or distributed, and the proposal would require congressional action. Estimates have put the potential cost at more than $1 trillion.The renewed $5,000 pledge comes as Trump has also announced a separate one-time payment of USD 90 to more than 20 million Medicare enrollees.The administration says the payment will help seniors cover part of their Medicare Part B premiums, with the money coming from the Medicare Improvement Fund.The Medicare payment is expected to be distributed through direct deposits or mailed checks, according to the administration. The standard monthly Medicare Part B premium for 2026 is $202.90, meaning the one-time payment would cover less than half of one month’s premium.Trump’s $5,000 proposal is separate from the Medicare payment and from the $500 refunds the administration has begun sending to nearly one million Americans over what it describes as excessive Affordable Care Act fees.The president has tied the $5,000 payment directly to the midterm election outcome, saying Republicans must win both chambers for the proposed dividend to be issued.The pledge has drawn scrutiny over its financing and whether such a payment could be authorised under existing law.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Saturday briefed a parliamentary consultative committee on India's \"multifaceted\" engagement with
articles.body: NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Saturday briefed a parliamentary consultative committee on India's "multifaceted" engagement with Russia, covering bilateral trade, investment and energy cooperation as well as New Delhi's diplomatic efforts to contribute towards ending the Ukraine conflict.Chairing the meeting on India-Russia relations, Jaishankar also informed members that Russia has agreed to take around 70,000 Indian skilled workers this year, particularly in construction and logistics, people familiar with the discussions said, according to news agency PTI.Jaishankar said India and Russia share an ambition to expand bilateral trade in a more balanced manner, including by increasing Indian exports to Russia across seven sectors — automobiles, pharmaceuticals, food, marine products, engineering goods, chemicals and textiles.Trade, connectivity and energy cooperationThe minister highlighted various areas of bilateral engagement, including trade, investments, energy, connectivity, culture and people-to-people ties, according to a social media post by Jaishankar.The discussions also covered an India-Eurasian Economic Union Free Trade Agreement, the Chennai-Vladivostok corridor, the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) and the Northern Sea Route.On energy cooperation, Jaishankar said India's priority was to safeguard the interests of Indian consumers."Our approach is to maintain multiple sources of supply," he said, according to people familiar with the meeting.The government has also been seeking to expand opportunities for Indian workers in Russia.Ukraine conflict and India's diplomatic effortsThe Ukraine conflict also featured prominently in the discussions, with Jaishankar apprising the panel of India's position and recent diplomatic efforts to support dialogue and diplomacy.In his social media post, Jaishankar said he highlighted India's "active support to dialogue & diplomacy to end the Ukraine conflict".The minister referred to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's August 31 meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Bishkek, where the PM said that "endless war must now give way to end of war".Jaishankar travelled to Ukraine last month and subsequently met the foreign ministers of Ukraine and Russia in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. During those engagements, he conveyed India's readiness to assist efforts to bring the conflict to an end, people familiar with the meeting said."If India can be of any help in any manner to bring the war to an end, it is ready to do so," Jaishankar said in his conversations.Putin's recent remarks at the Valdai Club in Moscow were also discussed. He had said Prime Minister Modi "has very good ideas for finding mutually acceptable solutions" to bring peace.Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha's remarks appreciating India's efforts were also noted during the meeting.Efforts to secure Indians in Russian militaryJaishankar also briefed the committee on the government's efforts to secure the release of Indian nationals serving in the Russian military.The government has engaged with Russian authorities, including at the highest levels, for the early discharge of such individuals, the people cited above said.So far, around 140 Indian nationals have been discharged, while India is in touch with Russian authorities regarding the whereabouts of 55 Indian nationals who are reportedly working for the Russian Arm.The government has also been taking action against agents who recruit Indians for such roles, with members being briefed about the risks faced by Indian citizens joining the Russian Army.The parliamentary committee meeting thus covered India's economic and energy engagement with Russia alongside its diplomatic efforts on Ukraine and its continuing efforts to secure the release of Indian nationals serving in the Russian military.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'He made a mistake but can't admit it': Russia's ex-PM says Putin 'not ready' to end Ukraine war
articles.summary: Russian president Vladimir Putin is not ready to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine despite growing economic pressures and unease among sections of
articles.body: Russian president Vladimir Putin is not ready to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine despite growing economic pressures and unease among sections of Russian society and the elite, former prime minister Mikhail Kasyanov said on Saturday.Kasyanov, who served as Russia’s prime minister from 2000 to 2004, said Putin understood that invading Ukraine in 2022 had been a mistake but remained unwilling to change course.“He made a mistake that he cannot bring himself to admit,” Kasyanov, 68, told AFP in Paris. “He believed the reports from his security services that Ukraine was weak.”Kasyanov said he was not convinced the war would end next year, arguing that high oil prices linked to the US-Iran conflict and disagreements between the United States and Europe over dealing with Moscow had strengthened Putin’s position.“Putin is, of course, rubbing his hands with glee,” he said. “He clearly believes he can continue the war without making any concessions. And he is convinced that he is winning a war of attrition against Ukraine.”The former prime minister warned that the coming winter could be particularly difficult for Ukraine and urged Western countries to apply “psychological pressure on the Kremlin” by maintaining unity and urgently supplying Kyiv with Patriot missile interceptors.Putin, a former KGB officer who turns 74 on Wednesday, has repeatedly said millions of Russians support the war. His ruling party won a record supermajority in elections last month, a result critics said followed a tightly controlled process.Kasyanov, who left Russia in 2022 and now lives in exile in Riga, said he remained in contact with members of the Russian ruling elite.“Fear reigns there -- I am talking about the ruling class,” he was quoted saying.“Everyone wants the war to end. An overwhelming majority does", he told AFP.He said views differed over how the conflict should conclude, with some seeking victory, others wanting Putin’s defeat and some simply wanting the fighting to stop.Among ordinary Russians, Kasyanov said he saw “no grounds for a revolt” despite casualties and rising food prices.“Russians have lived with high inflation for the past 30 years,” he said. “They have grown accustomed to putting up with it.”However, he warned that another large-scale mobilisation could trigger street protests.Kasyanov, who joined the opposition after being dismissed by Putin, described Russia as “practically totalitarian” and said there was “a sense of fatalism, hostility toward one another, and serious tension in society”.On Putin’s recent warning that Russia could use “all types of weapons” if Kaliningrad were attacked, Kasyanov urged Western countries not to be intimidated.“The West's and Europeans' biggest mistake is that they are too afraid of Putin. He is not as strong as he appears,” he said.“Putin fears the nuclear button more than many Europeans do.” Kasyanov said he did not believe Putin was preparing for open war with Europe, arguing that Moscow’s objective was to force European countries to acknowledge Russia.“What Putin wants is respect. He wants to force all of Europe to give it to him,” he said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: An Iowa family lived on and worked its farmland for 84 years as Tom Woods gradually expanded the operation; now 1,209 acres are being split into 13 tracts and auctioned, ending a family land chapter
articles.summary: For 84 years, the Woods family lived on and worked a growing patchwork of farmland near Randalia in northeast Iowa.
articles.body: For 84 years, the Woods family lived on and worked a growing patchwork of farmland near Randalia in northeast Iowa. Tom Woods, who grew up in the area, steadily added acres to the operation as properties and funds became available, raising grain and cattle while also helping run a family wholesale business. Now that long chapter is closing as 1,209 acres are divided into 13 tracts and put up for auction, a sale that land agents describe as rare for Fayette County and the wider region, according to a report by Agriculture.com. Read on to know more about it here:A lifetime of gradual expansionTom Woods built the portfolio over decades, acquiring land whenever the opportunity arose. He farmed the ground himself, producing grain and running cattle, while also contributing to Woods Brothers Wholesale Co., a business he founded with family members in the 1950s. His son worked alongside him on the farm from 1980 to 2014, ensuring that the next generation was deeply involved in day-to-day operations, as per Agriculture.com.The result was a well-maintained and highly productive set of farms. According to Peoples Company, the land has received extensive tile drainage, has a strong production history, and has benefited from conservation practices such as CRP buffer strips and waterway maintenance. That combination of careful stewardship and consistent investment has left the property in strong condition as it enters the market.Thirteen tracts across highly rated groundThe report further suggests that the 1,209.2-acre offering will be sold in 13 tracts ranging from about 53.7 to 172 acres each. Several of the more tillable parcels carry CSR2 ratings in the mid-80s, including Tract 1 at 85.0, Tract 2 at 84.6, Tract 3 at 84.5, and Tract 8 at 84.9. The CSR2 index, developed at Iowa State University, measures soil productivity and is widely used by buyers and lenders to compare farmland quality across the state.While much of the portfolio is geared toward row crop production, some tracts offer additional features. Tract 5 includes more than 34 acres of timber and frontage along the Volga River, appealing to buyers interested in recreation as well as farming. Tract 13 combines cropland with CRP acres and a large pond, adding further diversity to the mix.A hybrid auction in the Fayette Opera HouseThe sale will take place as a hybrid auction on Friday, October 30, at the Fayette Opera House in Fayette, Iowa, as per the report. Bidding will be conducted on a price-per-acre basis using the buyer's choice method, allowing the high bidder to select any or all available tracts at the winning bid. Bidding will continue until all 13 tracts have been sold, with the parcels not offered together as a single unit at the conclusion of the event.Peoples Company is handling the sale on behalf of the Thomas J. and Carolyn J. Woods Trust. Senior land agent Travis Smock said offerings of this scale are uncommon in northeast Iowa, noting that only a handful of landowners in each county own portfolios of this size. He expects strong interest from local farmers as well as investors, hunters, and recreational buyers.Why this sale stands out in northeast IowaFayette County does not frequently see large, multi-tract farmland auctions of this magnitude. Smock told Agriculture.com that it is very rare for a property of this significance to be offered in the county or anywhere in the region. The combination of size, soil quality, and improved drainage makes the Woods land particularly attractive to operators looking to expand their acreage.At the same time, the recreational elements add another layer of appeal. Timbered ground, river frontage, and pond features draw interest from buyers who want a mix of income-producing cropland and personal use land. That dual demand can help sustain competitive bidding even when broader market conditions are uncertain.The end of a family eraFor the Woods family, the auction marks the conclusion of an 84-year relationship with the land. Tom Woods raised his family on these farms, worked them through changing commodity cycles, and passed on farming knowledge to his son. The decision to sell does not erase that history but rather brings it to a defined close, allowing the next owners to write their own chapter.Smock noted that the Woods land has been very well maintained, with significant tiling, strong yields, and attention to soil health. That legacy of care is likely to reassure buyers that they are acquiring ground that has been managed with a long-term perspective. For many in the local community, the sale will also serve as a reminder of how deeply farm families are tied to the places they work.What buyers are watching this fallThe Woods auction is part of a busy October for Iowa farmland, with more than 10,300 acres scheduled for sale across 34 counties. Rabail Chandio, an assistant professor of economics at Iowa State University, said harvest yields, commodity prices, interest rates, government payments, and the amount of land coming to market will all shape results through the end of the year. Farms with strong soils and good drainage tend to attract attention even when margins are tight.Local supply also matters. When several farms come up for sale in the same county at the same time, buyers have more choices and that can affect prices. The opposite can happen when a desirable property reaches the market in an area with few other options, keeping competition strong among nearby operators. The Woods sale, given its size and quality, is likely to draw focused attention from those looking to secure ground in northeast Iowa.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Saturday said the Ukrainian forces have so far “de-occupied” about 125-140 square kilometres of territory under operation “Vivaldi”.“As of today, about 125-140 square kilometres have been de-occupied,” Zelensky said.Operation Vivaldi is a name given by Ukraine’s armed forces to an ongoing counteroffensive in the Lyman direction in northern Donetsk region.Speaking in an interview with Reuters, Zelensky said the operation was “not finished yet” and claimed that Russian casualties had increased over the past two to three months.He claimed Russia had suffered 42,000 casualties a month during the recent period, compared with 30,000-32,000 casualties per month since the beginning of the year.Zelensky said Ukraine’s military had wanted to begin the operation a year earlier but that it had not been sufficiently prepared at the time.“Thank God, we decided to postpone it a bit, and now we have good results and fewer losses,” he said.On US efforts to end the war, Zelensky said he believed President Donald Trump wanted to stop Russia’s war against Ukraine.“I think the US really wants to stop Russia’s war. I trust them,” he said, while adding that it was difficult to stop a big country that “doesn't want to stop”.Zelensky said the US was seeking compromises with Russia but argued that time was being lost in pursuing them.He said Trump wanted to achieve “some kind of victory” before the US midterm elections, while claiming Russian President Vladimir Putin would seek to make the situation “non-negotiable”.Russia-Ukraine exchange long-range strikesOn Saturday morning, a Russian Shahed drone struck Kyiv’s Pivnichnyi Bridge, amid Moscow’s attempts to dismantle Kyiv’s infrastructure all around.“Overnight, residential buildings, railways, and energy infrastructure in many regions came under Russian attack. In Chornomorsk, a drone struck a vessel,” Zelensky wrote on X.According to Zelensky, Ukraine’s long-range capabilities had struck targets in the Samara region and positions of Russian forces operating Iskander missile systems in the Bryansk region. He also said there were “new results in the Black Sea”.Meanwhile, in a notice issued on Saturday, the Russian foreign ministry said its forces were continuing to carry out “systematic and sustained strikes” against military targets in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.The ministry said the strikes were in response to what it described as “terrorist attacks by the Armed Forces of Ukraine against Russia’s civilian population and infrastructure”.It also reiterated a previous call for foreign nationals and diplomatic personnel in Kyiv to leave the city and refrain from travelling to Ukraine. articles.title: 'Crazy' FlyDubai landing explained by Israeli pilot, who offers steps to prevent future crises
articles.summary: Eliran Almog, a former Israeli pilot and aviation cybersecurity CEO, explains why FlyDubai flight 1073's emergency landing was nearly impossible.
articles.body: Eliran Almog, a former Israeli helicopter pilot turned aviation cybersecurity firm CEO, explained just how "crazy" it was that the near-hijacked FlyDubai flight 1073 managed to land safely after a violent midair attack. "You can't imagine being in that position. You see the videos, you hear the kids screaming, and people don't necessarily understand what is happening," the former Israeli Air Force pilot told Fox News Digital. After an Omani national copilot — who has since been identified as 29-year-old Hamam al-Hammami — allegedly stabbed FlyDubai flight 1073’s pilot Capt. Smit Machchhar mid-flight, the aircraft plummeted more than 14,000 feet in 30 seconds. "The g-force on the plane was enormous, and you basically think you are going to die," Almog said, adding "it's crazy that the aircraft did not break up in the air, and landing it with the tail damage it sustained was remarkable." FLYDUBAI PASSENGER SAYS CO-PILOT STABBED CAPTAIN BEFORE TERRIFYING PLUNGE, EMERGENCY LANDING Despite sustaining serious injuries, Machchhar was able to hit a button to open the cockpit door, allowing Israeli passengers to rush into the cockpit and subdue al-Hammami, officials said. A second FlyDubai crew that happened to be aboard the craft then stabilized the plane and successfully completed an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. FLYDUBAI PILOT SHOWED WORLD 'THE HIGHEST FORM OF COURAGE,' INDIA'S PM SAYS "As a pilot, if I were in this situation, I'm not sure I could have landed the aircraft. Every commercial aircraft is different, requiring different setup, landing procedures and limitations," Almog explained. Almog, who now advises airliners and adjacent businesses on how to shore up their cybersecurity, explained how crucial it was for carriers to ensure their pilots undergo thorough screening processes for both psychological and potential political risks. FLYDUBAI CO-PILOT ACCUSED OF STABBING CAPTAIN IDENTIFIED AS 29-YEAR-OLD OMANI NATIONAL "We give a lot of weight in the process to the characteristics of the pilot. The technical and cognitive skills are important, but we make sure that the pilot is balanced and resilient in extreme cases," he said. "Because aviation is critical infrastructure, we must rethink how we screen pilots — not just initially, but continuously. Even for experienced pilots, we need the right tools in place to identify when someone is facing family issues, psychological distress, or developing extreme views that could impose risk. These are practices the industry needs to adopt, and I call on governments and regulators to step in," he continued. PILOT’S SUDDEN DEATH DURING OVERNIGHT LAYOVER PUTS SPOTLIGHT ON FATIGUE CONCERNS While numerous countries, including Israel and Saudi Arabia, are conducting their own investigations into al-Hammami and the FlyDubai incident, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox & Friends in a Thursday interview that the copilot had been exposed to "Islamist radical indoctrination." President Donald Trump, meanwhile, suggested the pilot could have been trained or motivated by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). TRUMP’S IRAN CRACKDOWN COLLIDES WITH NATO ALLY SEEKING ACCESS TO AMERICA’S PRIZED FIGHTER JET Almog told Fox News Digital that geopolitical concerns, such as the ones imposed by the ongoing wars in the Middle East, are increasingly becoming airlines' top risk factor for a number of reasons. articles.title: In 1834, the O'Connor family's Texas ranching legacy began; 191 years later, an $8.863 million deal protected 6,409 acres of coastal prairie while keeping it a working cattle ranch
articles.summary: A Texas ranching legacy that began in 1834 is now tied to one of the state's major private-land conservation efforts.
articles.body: A Texas ranching legacy that began in 1834 is now tied to one of the state's major private-land conservation efforts. An $8.863 million conservation easement has permanently protected approximately 6,409 acres of the historic T.M. O'Connor Ranch in Goliad County, according to The Nature Conservancy (TNC). The agreement safeguards one of the largest remaining intact stretches of coastal prairie in Texas while allowing the O'Connor family to continue operating the property as a working cattle ranch. The deal was supported by federal RESTORE funding, along with private contributions, creating a model in which historic ranching and long-term habitat protection continue on the same land.A ranching legacy dating to 1834The O'Connor family's connection to the property reaches back nearly two centuries. TNC says the family first established its ranching legacy in the region in 1834, eventually assembling a much larger landholding of about 600,000 acres. Much of that legacy remains under O'Connor family management today. The newly protected acreage forms part of the Refugio-Goliad Prairie, an important coastal landscape in southeast Texas. TNC describes the area as one of the state's remaining large intact coastal prairie systems, with grasslands, marshes and other habitats that have become increasingly scarce.The conservation agreement does not transfer the ranch into public ownership. Instead, it places restrictions on future development and habitat fragmentation while allowing the family to retain ownership and continue ranching. TNC says the property will remain a private working cattle ranch under the O'Connor family's stewardship.$8.863 million conservation dealThe conservation easement was purchased for $8.863 million, according to TNC. Of that amount, $7.6 million came through a grant administered by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) as the state's representative to the Gulf Coast Ecosystem Restoration Council, or RESTORE Council. TNC provided the remaining funds with support from the Knobloch Family Foundation, Frank Klein and H-E-B.The project is significant because it represents the first conservation easement approved by the RESTORE Council and the largest land-protection deal in the Gulf region funded through the RESTORE Act, according to TNC. The federal programme uses money derived from civil penalties related to the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill for projects involving ecological restoration, coastal protection, economic development and community resilience.Steven Schar, deputy executive director of TCEQ and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott's designee to the RESTORE Council, described the agreement as a major milestone for Texas and the Gulf Coast. He said in TNC's announcement that the easement would keep critical coastal habitat intact for future generations.Protecting one of Texas' rare coastal prairiesThe conservation easement covers a landscape that supports a variety of wildlife and plant species. According to TNC, the ranch provides habitat for more than 300 species and is among the most important areas in the United States for migrating, wintering and breeding shorebirds. The prairie also provides habitat for species of conservation concern, including the Attwater's prairie chicken, black rail and Sprague's pipit. Rare plants found in the wider landscape include the Refugio rain lily and Welder machaeranthera.The Refugio rain lily is particularly notable because it is found only in Refugio and Goliad counties in Texas. Protecting large, connected areas of prairie can therefore help retain habitat for species that depend on this increasingly limited ecosystem. Texas' coastal prairies have declined dramatically over time. These grasslands and marshes once covered about 6 million acres; today, less than 5% of the state's coastal prairie remains.Conservation without ending ranchingThe O'Connor Ranch agreement is designed around the idea that conservation does not necessarily require removing land from agricultural use. The easement prevents development and fragmentation while allowing cattle operations to continue. The protected grassland also provides environmental functions beyond wildlife habitat. TNC says intact coastal prairie can help buffer communities from flooding and hurricanes, improve air and water quality and store carbon in its extensive root systems.The ranch's management will continue to incorporate conservation considerations. TNC's Texas annual report says the management plan includes collaboration with Texas A&M University's Department of Rangeland, Wildlife and Fisheries Management and its Center for Grazinglands and Ranch Management, bringing research, guidance and monitoring to the long-term stewardship of the prairie.A permanent layer of protectionFor the O'Connor family, the easement adds a new chapter to a ranching history that has lasted since the 19th century. For conservation organisations and public agencies, it permanently protects a substantial portion of one of Texas' remaining coastal prairie landscapes. Jeff Francell, associate director of land protection for TNC in Texas, said in the organisation's announcement that the project represents both a major permanent protection effort in Texas' largest intact coastal prairie and the first conservation easement purchased with RESTORE funding.The result is a property where cattle ranching and habitat conservation will continue side by side. Rather than converting the land to a new use, the easement places long-term limits on development while allowing the historic ranching operation to continue, preserving both the family's agricultural legacy and a significant stretch of Texas coastal prairie.You use AI every day. articles.body: At a time when several Indian students and professionals in the US are staring at an uncertain future because of visa issues and the ongoing crackdown on OPT programs, Indian techie Aditya Kumar Thota shared his experience of getting laid off, looking for jobs in the US, then coming back to India without a job, and then landing a job with a US company in India within 40 days.In a YouTube interview with Pritesh Jagani's education and career podcast, Aditya explained his situation -- how his decision to come back to India was supported by his family and how he did not have a huge financial burden. He said he realized that he was just surviving in the US and not actually living. In Hyderabad, on the other hand, he said he stays with his parents, has their own house and his savings are also going up.Apart from India's weather and traffic, the Indian techie who is now working as a project manager with Dun and Bradstreet said there is nothing much he has been missing much.Thota explained that he came to the US for his master's at East Texas A&M University in 2023. He started working for Capital One on his OPT but on the last day of his OPT, he said he was laid off. It was in July 2025 and he got another job, though he started preparing mentally for returning to India. He said between July and November 2025, he got several offers but none of those materialized because of the visa sponsorship issue. It was also the time when the Donald Trump administration announced the $100K H-1B visa fee. The visa fee is still blocked by court orders but it created a lot of confusion and deterred many companies from hiring people on H-1B visa.Thota said he waited for the last chance of H-1B this year in March but then he wrapped up his US stay and came back to India. He said he started looking for Indian jobs in the US only but the active search started after he landed in India. Within around 40 days, he got a job in India."If you are thinking to come back to India, don't see it as a failure. Things are not in our hands. articles.title: Road injuries 10th leading cause for deaths in India: WHO report
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: ‘Road injuries’ was the eighth leading cause of deaths among males in India in 2023, and in the case of females, ‘falls’ was the eighth biggest
articles.body: NEW DELHI: ‘Road injuries’ was the eighth leading cause of deaths among males in India in 2023, and in the case of females, ‘falls’ was the eighth biggest cause of deaths, as per the latest WHO Global Health Estimates (GHE). Overall, road traffic injuries ranked the 10th leading cause of death for both males and females in India, while fatalities due to falls ranked 9th.India, which has recorded the maximum road deaths since such global data compilation started, registered 1.74 lakh such fatalities in 2023, and this was a little over 14% of the 12.2 lakh people who lost their lives in road crashes across the world. This has only increased in the past two years to reach 1.83 lakh in 2025. The figures underline the continuing scale of the road safety challenge in the country, where road crashes claim 500 lives daily.Falls in India claimed 25,150 lives, as per the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) data, which was around 3% of the total 8.42 lakh lives lost in such incidents. Most of the deaths due to road crashes and falls are preventable. The data also highlights the significant burden of injuries that can result in loss of life and have wider social and economic consequences for families.As per the WHO report, globally, road traffic injuries were the 8th biggest cause of death in low-income countries and the 10th biggest in middle-income countries. Globally, it was ranked 11th, indicating that the high number of such deaths not only has a huge burden on low- and middle-income countries but also a major concern for the global community, despite many developed nations having been successful in bringing down fatalities due to road crashes. The differences in rankings across income groups also reflect the varying burden of road injuries across countries and regions.Road safety experts have maintained that low- and middle-income countries need to find solutions to this “avoidable disaster” taking into account the local conditions, including heterogeneous road users and poorly sensitised authorities about the concept of safety of all users. They said addressing the problem would require greater attention to the safety needs of different categories of road users and a stronger focus on preventing crashes and reducing their consequences.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
